title: Loudspeaker
subtitle: Turns an electrical signal into sound
summary: A loudspeaker is a coil of wire in a magnetic gap, glued to a paper cone. Current in the coil becomes a force along the axis; the cone pushes air; air is sound. The magnet does not move. The cone does, a millimetre or two, thousands of times a second.

parts.name: Cone
parts.short: The piston that pushes the air
parts.detail: A light, stiff flare of paper or plastic. Light so it can accelerate; stiff so it does not break up into ripples at high frequencies. Its area is the reason a speaker can move a roomful of air with a millimetre of travel.

parts.name: Surround
parts.detail: A roll of rubber or foam that lets the cone move in and out without leaking air around the edge. It is a seal and a spring. When it rots, the speaker starts to sound flabby, then tears.

parts.name: Dust Cap
parts.short: Keeps grit out of the gap
parts.detail: A small dome over the voice coil. Dust in the magnetic gap will scrape, then jam. The cap also radiates the highest frequencies, which is why a dented one changes the treble.

parts.name: Voice Coil
parts.short: The motor winding, wound on the former
parts.detail: Turns of copper in the gap between pole piece and magnet. Current through it, in a radial field, produces an axial force — Fleming's left-hand rule at audio speed. Too much current and it cooks; the smell of a blown speaker is this varnish burning.

parts.name: Coil Former
parts.short: The tube the coil is wound on
parts.detail: Kapton, aluminium or paper. It has to be stiff, heat-proof, and exactly centred in a gap a millimetre wide. If it rubs, you hear it as a scrape on bass notes.

parts.name: Spider
parts.short: Centres the coil and springs it back
parts.detail: A corrugated cloth disc. It holds the coil dead in the middle of the gap and provides most of the restoring force that makes the cone a resonant system. Stiffer spider, higher resonant frequency, tighter bass.

parts.name: Magnet
parts.short: The field the coil pushes against
parts.detail: A ferrite or neodymium ring. It does not move. Its only job is to put a strong radial field across the gap so that current in the coil becomes force along the axis. Bigger magnet, more force for the same current — efficiency.

parts.name: Pole Piece
parts.short: Shapes the gap the coil lives in
parts.detail: A steel T: a centre pole and a front plate. Together with the magnet they make a narrow cylindrical gap with field lines running inward. The coil sits in that gap. The geometry of this T is most of a driver's motor.

parts.name: Basket
parts.detail: A stamped or cast frame. It holds the magnet, the spider and the surround concentric. If it flexes, the coil rubs. The spokes are there so the cone can breathe from behind — a sealed basket is a different speaker.

parts.name: Terminals
parts.detail: Two lugs on the back. From here a tinsel lead runs up to the coil, flexible enough to survive millions of strokes. Reverse them and the cone moves in when it should move out — polarity, which only matters once you have two speakers.

steps.title: A coil in a gap
steps.body: The voice coil sits in a thin cylindrical gap where the magnet's field runs inward. Current in the coil, field across it: the force is along the axis.

steps.title: The cone is the piston
steps.body: That force is glued to a paper flare. The flare's area is large, its travel is small, and that is how a watt of electricity becomes a roomful of sound.

steps.title: Hinges, not slop
steps.body: The surround at the rim and the spider behind the coil let the cone move only in and out, and spring it back. Anything else is a scrape.

steps.title: The basket keeps the gap true
steps.body: All of this hangs from a chassis that has to stay concentric for the life of the driver. A bent basket is a ruined motor.

steps.title: Current in, air out
steps.body: The amplifier arrives at two lugs. Reverse them and the piston inhales when it should exhale. With one speaker you may not notice. With two, the bass cancels.

quiz.prompt: Tap the winding that turns current into force.
Why does the magnet not move?
choices: The force is on the coil, which is in the gap; the magnet only supplies the field
It is glued to the cone
It is an electromagnet that turns off
quiz.explain: A loudspeaker is a linear motor. The moving part is the coil. The magnet is the stator.

quiz.prompt: Tap the corrugated cloth that centres the coil in the gap.
Tap the piston that actually pushes the air.
What happens if the coil is not centred in the gap?
choices: It rubs, scrapes, and eventually jams
quiz.explain: The gap is about a millimetre. Off-centre is a scrape on every bass note.

quiz.prompt: Tap the steel part that, with the magnet, forms the gap.
